newsitem.title: UK: Hole in heart could mean brain damage for divers.
newsitem.headline: Hole in heart could mean brain damage for divers.

text.p: A tiny hole in the heart that affects about a quarter of all people could be letting through gas bubbles that cause brain damage in scuba divers, researchers said on Friday.

Michael Knauth and colleagues at the University of Heidelberg found that some frequent divers who seem to be perfectly healthy have brain lesions -- and those with the tiny hole are at most risk of the brain damage.
The hole, known as a foramen ovale, exists in the heart when a foetus is developing. It keeps blood from going to the lungs which are not used while a baby is in the womb.
It usually closes at birth but in about a quarter of the population it stays open to some degree. In some cases the opening is big enough to let blood clots or air bubbles through.

Knowing this, Knauth's team set out to see if the hole could be letting gas bubbles into the brains of divers. They recruited 87 divers with an average of more than 500 dives each -- who would be professional or serious amateur divers -- and used magnetic resonance imaging to look at their brains.
"A total of 41 brain lesions were detected in 11 of the 87 divers," they wrote in a report in the British Medical Journal.

"The three divers with multiple brain lesions were non-smokers, aged in their 40s, and did not have any other multiple risk factors." What was different was that they had the little holes -- the foramen ovales.

"The association of multiple brain lesions with a large patent foramen ovale supports the hypothesis that the brain lesions were due to arterial gas embolism during or shortly after decompression," they wrote.

Peter Wilmshurst, a cardiac consultant at the Royal Shrewsbury Hospital in central England, said divers could quit -- or there were other options, including staying in shallower water and not staying down as long as other divers.

"If you are someone whose whole livelihood or social setup depends on diving you may modify things in a different way," he said. Ultrasound scans could show whether divers had the foramen -- and they could choose to have surgery to close it.
Divers use compressed air -- either a mixture like regular air that is 70 percent nitrogen and 30 percent oxygen or, if they go deeper, a mixture including helium.
But this compressed air can cause bubbles that stay inside the body if they are not very careful -- and can cause damage if they come up too quickly.
